title: Is that fair?
author: Upbeat_Ad_6119
selftext:
Loving something but hating it just because AI was involved. That’s what’s really lame, in my opinion.

I'm the only one who can hate my self for that, lol.. I wanna have all skills to do games even without AI, but unfortunately, I don't. I'm just learning how to code games, and it's a long process.. Art and sound, is something that I never could learn at all, It's just not my thing. That's why in all my games I'm keeping visuals and sounds extremely simple. But for someone that's still problem.

My controversial opinion (or maybe not that much): bad AI-made games get way less hate than good ones.

EDIT: [https://nebitula.itch.io/blotosis](https://nebitula.itch.io/blotosis) adding the game link here, as one commenter asked for it..

EDIT V2: I have updated the page with organic text, if someone may wonder..

replies.author: Hot_Professional8287
replies.body:
It's not the typical reframe or triplet pattern that we saw in the earlier AI days. Claude has this way of always talking like he's a moody artist in a dark, New York slam poetry lounge on open-mic night. He always has this clever little "setup" where he suspends your attention and then delivers the meaning at the very end (*the "slam" to his poetry*).

*>Divide again and you are steering four cells, then eight, all with the same keys, each going its own way.*

Do you see how the concept is "dragged" out with this staccato of statements about the nature of the thing? ..and then the payload/meaning is at the end, expressed with a poetic twist? It's like a consistent "suspension" of the idea (*Claude holds it in the air, grabbing your attention*), and then Claude finally reveals it with a little poetic flourish. Slam.

*>Ink-and-water sounds and a soft tune, all synthesised.*

The thing (*for what purpose?*)... the slam.

*>Every level starts with 400 ink, and only the ink that ends up inside the circles counts.*

This one's very subtle, but it still has the same telltale setup pattern. A setup with an unclear conclusion.. then a little poetic slam delivering the meaning.

It's dramatic, and I think it's effective at keeping the reader's attention because it's such an unusual way to speak (*to me, at least*). Claude's a poet (*Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, Fable*), and everyone is suddenly speaking in slam poetry.

comments.author: EducationSpare6425
comments.body:
You said you are learning to code games. Well, one of the core skills you must build is to take negative feedback, no matter the quality and subjectivit, and not get discouraged. 
In fact, you must find a way to always turn it into something productive. How you can do that:
1. Find something constructive in the feedback. If necessary - follow up with the provider. Or reach out to them with a questionnaire in the first place.
2. Get... angry. And then transform that anger into motivation. Let "I'll show them" be the driver for your next attempt or the next consumed book on the topic.
3. At the very least take it as a metric data point. Later compare how the number and ratio of such feedbacks has changed. That can show you if you are going in the right direction.

replies.author: GrandPaladin
replies.body:
The honest answer is that ideas have always been cheap, and the bar is higher - recognize that its higher and deliver higher if you want respect!

You didn’t make this game for a decade- AI hasnt even been out that long. Even if your game was in development and ideation for that long, you’ve sold yourself quite short here by trying to market and take the easy way out for areas that are critical to a games success (aka the cover of the book and advertisement that get people hooked).

I can understand how you feel about putting in a lot of effort developing and ideating… but you do need to understand that Players/Users have had to deal with game companies pulling fast ones over them since their inception- whether that’s microtransactions or ads or whatever, players are harsh critics, and that’s fair given that we as game developers are asking for hours of their time and their love for games to be spent on something that is ours.

Golden rule, do unto others as you would want done to you. If you want the players to earnestly look and try to love your game, you need to put an equal amount of love and effort into the other areas that will get them to the gameplay and make them feel welcomed.

Its 2026 and anyone can ask AI, make me a game ad summary. You can ask ChatGPT how to make game ads or how to make designs or search up YouTube videos and tutorials. The content and teachings are there… do not use your inexperience as a crutch when asking, hat in hand, for players to try to play your game.

Put some polish into this game you love for damn sake.

So it sounds like the problem is not that AI was used, but that you never took the time to re-write the user facing English prose that was left behind and took its output verbatim and posted.

Lets say you can't code, but you're creative. That's a fair use case for AI, right? At least show effort by re-writing what you can as a human—whether that's English, Spanish, French, or some other language.

One of the first ways to contribute to a project even as a non-coder is peer reviewing documentation to make sure it is readable, accurate, and free of typos. Everyone can do that. If you at least do that for your AI's output, you will receive a lot less backlash.

replies.author: P_kyuu_juu
replies.body:
Your words: "i mean creating the assets for tripple-A and drawing some pixel art is not the same"

And on pixel art vs high poly 3D art: conveying small actions, emotions and details is SO much harder with pixel art than it is with a detailed 3D model. You say it doesn't need as much precision, but it's the opposite. Every pixel carries much more weight because of the limited resolution you're working with, and it requires a lot of skill and experience to get the most out of it. AI would not get you those results.

I'll leave it at that because I think we're not going to agree on this and I don't feel like arguing any further
